name: Flame

facts.text: Level 64, 7,000 health, a ghostly fire in the Cursed Forest that casts Flame Strike (300 heat).
A second Flame rises when Luriquay dies.

In the Dindshenchas of Uisnech, Mide son of Brath lights the first fire in Ireland for the sons of Nemed; it blazes seven years, every chief fire is kindled from it, a sack of grain and a pig are paid for each, and Mide buries the tongues of the druids who object.
Living Server lore: the court hearth lit from a brand of Uisnech's line, a fire no one at the stones had the right to put out.

story:
Fire burns on nothing in the Cursed Forest, and the oldest of those fires has a mind. At the heart of the court wood there was a hearth, the Sylvan say, where the bright folk and the dark folk sat on opposite sides of one fire and bargained across it. On the night the bargain broke, nobody put the fire out. Nobody fed it either. It did not go out.

Flame is that hearth-fire, wandering. It drifts between the trees as a ghost-fire, burning on bare earth, feeding on nothing, and it strikes at anything warm enough to be worth burning. It is small, as such things go, and its strikes are sharp. The Sylvan say it is lonely. It has found company in Luriquay, the lurikeen who drank from the court wood's fires; when Luriquay falls, a second flame rises from him, and the Sylvan think that one is a spark of this one, carried in him all these years. Two fires, one hearth.

The druids say that if both fires are ever put out on the same night, the court wood may start, very slowly, to heal. Nobody has yet managed it on purpose.

The druids of Lough Gur say the hearth of the court wood was not lit from nothing. Every chief hearth in Hibernia was kindled once from one fire, the lore of Uisnech tells. Mide, of the people of Nemed, lit the first fire on the hill of Uisnech, and it blazed for seven years, and every chief hearth in the land was lit from it, and for each hearth he took a sack of grain and a pig. The druids of that age said his fire was an insult to them. Mide had their tongues cut out and buried in the hill, and sat on the place.

The druids of Lough Gur tell that tale against their own order more cheerfully than a stranger would expect. They say the court hearth was lit from a brand of Uisnech's line, carried from hearth to hearth across the realm until it reached the bargaining stones, so that the courts would bargain at a fire older than either of them. When the bargain broke there was no one left with the right to put it out, because no one at the stones owned it. It went on burning as a guest's fire burns after the host has gone to bed, and at some hour of that long night it got up and left the hearth.
legend: A small fight with a sharp bite: its strikes are heat, so wards against heat help. It is weak to anything that puts out fire. Watch out when you kill Luriquay nearby, because another Flame rises from him, and two fires at once is how small groups die. Wards against heat and quick damage. Superstition: never cook over a fire in the Cursed Forest. It might be this one. Nicknames: 'the hearth', 'the little fire'. Bands who do Flame and Luriquay on the same night say the forest feels lighter afterward. Superstition: never lay a torch on bare ground near the forest's heart, or Flame takes it as an invitation.

aggro: Sit by the hearth. Bargain with me.
death: The fire goes out without smoke.

loremasterTopic.text: The ghost of a hearth-fire from the night the court wood broke. It burns on nothing and strikes at anything warm.

bookPage: From Derbáil of Ardee's list: grandmother said there was a hearth at the heart of the court wood, with the bright folk on one side and the dark folk on the other, and that on the night the bargain broke nobody put the fire out. It has been burning on nothing ever since and walking about. Never cook over a fire in the Cursed Forest, she said, because you do not know whose fire it is. I have never cooked in any forest since. My husband thinks this is foolish. My husband has never seen a fire walk. She said, too, that every chief hearth in the land was lit once from the fire on Uisnech, so mind whose fire you sit beside.
